articles.title: Shrinking degree premium
articles.content: UNIVERSITIES were originally established as centres of higher learning, places to pursue knowledge, not wages. The Abbasid-era Bayt al-Hikmah (House of Wisdom) in Baghdad brought together scholars who translated Greek, Persian, Indian, and Syriac works on philosophy, medicine, and astronomy into Arabic, and courts in Cordoba and Cairo built great libraries of their own to attract innovative thinkers. In England, the University of Cambridge has, for over 800 years, been at the centre of education, innovation, and intellectual debate, shaping some of the greatest minds in history, such as Isaac Newton, Charles Darwin, Alan Turing, Bertrand Russell, John Maynard Keynes, and Stephen Hawking. Across the Atlantic, Harvard has since at least the 19th century championed reason, research, and intellectual freedom. By the mid-20th century, its mission had widened to academic excellence, research dominance and democratic access through merit-based admission, and the university degree had become the passport to a profession. Today’s teenagers and their parents see it differently. They pursue a degree for its economic value, and employers treat it as a signal of advanced, scarce skills. Both assumptions were long taken for granted, but both are now in doubt. Claudia Goldin and Lawrence Katz, in their work on the ‘race between education and technology’, showed that more education does not automatically meet more demand for skills. The information revolution sustained a four-decade boom in knowledge jobs, so that the graduate premium rose even as the number of graduates grew. That long phase now appears to be ending. Recent research by José Azar, Mireia Giné, and Javier Sanz-Espín finds that the US wage premium for college graduates fell steadily between 2022 and 2026, returning to its mid-1990s level, a total drop of about eight per cent. In the UK, the FT’s John Burn-Murdoch reports a similar pattern, with a sharp fall even among STEM graduates and in London’s knowledge economy, despite a slowdown in the share of young people going to university. What makes this striking is that it is not a story of too many graduates. Supply has levelled off in both countries, which would ordinarily push the premium up. The fall is taken as weaker demand, attributing about 28pc of it to the exposure of white-collar occupations to generative AI, although the link is not proven to be causal. Whatever the cause, the equation of academic achievement and economic value looks like the relic of a passing era. To change how our society views skills, we need to bring them into the formal education system. Pakistan’s own system shows the strain. The country has 278 recognised universities and degree-awarding institutions, of which 163 are public, accommodating roughly 85pc of active students. The Higher Education Commission has permitted a rapid growth of private universities, many of them thinly resourced, which enrol thousands of students for revenue, so that their graduates struggle to compete with those of elite institutions. University enrolment, which peaked at 2.23 million, fell to about 1.96m in 2024-25, a drop of around 12pc, or more than 260,000 students, in three years. Even after eligibility criteria were relaxed, 743 of 22,300 medical and dental places remained vacant in 2025-26. The fall has been blamed on inflation, rising fees, reduced government spending, and doubts about what a degree now returns. If the university degree is no longer the certain route to a livelihood, Pakistan needs a credible alternative, and the evidence points to skills-based training. Yet our technical and vocational education and training (TVET) sector is beset by systemic weaknesses: outdated syllabuses, poorly equipped workshops, instructors with little industry exposure, inadequate funding, and certificates that neither employers nor foreign labour markets trust. The result is a severe gap between the skills industry needs and what the system supplies. Demand-side barriers make it worse. Because of social stigma attached to manual and technical trades, families favour academic degrees and secure government jobs that offer regular increments, pension and opportunities for corruption, so participation is low, and even lower among women. Responsibility is also divided between the federal body, National Vocational and Technical Training Commission (NAVTTC) and provincial authorities, TEVTA, producing inconsistent policies and fragmented oversight. To change how our society views skills, we need to bring them into the formal education system on a large scale, using the network of 250,000 public and private schools and 11,000 colleges to teach skills alongside the standard curriculum. Chief ministers should champion this change and lead the effort personally. To bring scale and rigour to the sector, NAVTTC should evolve from a traditional regulator into a dynamic, market-driven facilitator, taking its cue from systems the world regards as vocational success stories. Germany and Switzerland train young people inside firms to standards set with industry, so that apprenticeships carry the same esteem as a degree. Germany’s ‘dual system’ splits a student’s time between vocational school and real-world company work, and the Swiss vocational system is prestigious and market responsive. Singapore’s Institute of Technical Education shows how state leadership and funding tied to employment outcomes can raise the status of technical education. Forging binding, legally structured partnerships, beyond MOUs, with global TVET leaders can systematically transform the entire training ecosystem. NAVTTC could partner with the Swiss Federal University for Vocational Education and Training to overhaul instructor training, adopt a German-style apprenticeship policy to build an industry-driven, dual vocational training system across Pakistan, and establish a joint venture with Singapore’s ITE Education Services to design and audit digital training centres. A degree will remain valuable for those who can afford it and use it well. But a country cannot build its future on a credential whose price keeps rising while its worth declines. Pakistan should teach its young people the skills the economy will pay for, from the trades to communication, IT, AI, entrepreneurship and leadership, including for graduates. That would free universities from producing mass job certificates and let them return to their founding purpose: to nurture reasoning, scholarship, philosophy, innovation and the liberal arts, and to shape independent minds and original thinkers. The writer holds a PhD degree in economics from the University of Cambridge, and is the author of The Shady Economics of International Aid. He has served as chief economist of the State Bank of Pakistan and senior adviser at the IMF.
articles.author: Saeed Ahmed

articles.title: New provinces, old solutions
articles.content: MANY years ago, a senior official of a multilateral development bank delivered a harsh indictment of Pakistan’s state of affairs: it is a seriously large country run by a succession of non-serious policymaking elite. While the setting for the delivery of this critique was an informal one, it left one pondering its accuracy. Sadly, Pakistan’s ruling elites, irrespective of the political flag they bear, regularly try and prove the gentleman right. The recent spate of political statements on the creation of new provinces serves as an example. Administrative boundaries are not sacrosanct and must be viewed as mechanisms designed to serve evolving and defined public interest. Speaking about the creation of new provinces is not, therefore, tantamount to a conspiracy. Rather it reflects a healthy approach to reassessing their utility and viability. That said, restructuring a federation is not a trifling matter as its implications run deep and wide — from the obvious fiscal imperatives and changes to the balance of political representation, to the everyday impact on public service delivery and on the lives of citizens. Hasty, discordant political sound bites cannot, therefore, be a substitute for rigorous, extensive, and inclusive deliberation and analysis. The experience of other nations in this respect, including several where the author has had the privilege of leading the process, is instructive. There are two common strands of note. First, there is no single model to follow and changes are rooted in legal, political, and economic contexts. Second, political motives aside, each effort identified specific problems that the change was intended to solve. India’s establishment of Telangana was characterised by strong institutional arrangements, and extensive public engagement over an 11-month period. Brazil’s division of Goiás to form Tocantins responded to a long-standing public movement and leveraged constitutionally mandated plebiscitary mechanisms for public consent. In Russia, consolidation rather than fragmentation served as the principle for establishing the Zabaykalsky Krai region, with improved living standards being a clearly defined objective. Accelerating socioeconomic development was also the raison d’être for Timor-Leste’s establishment of the world’s newest Special Administrative Region in Oé-Cusse. From these and other global experiences, one can distill several insights and lessons for Pakistan. Lesson 1: Never treat the issue of creating new regions as merely redrawing the map. This reductive approach will upend any potential benefits that might accrue from a careful and considered process of reviewing how government is structured. The era of arbitrary, extractive cartography — for example, the Radcliffe Line, the Sykes-Picot Agreement, and Cecil Rhodes’s British South Africa Company — is dead and should stay that way. Pakistan should frame the issue of new provinces not as a form of territorial re-engineering but as a fundamental state reform aimed at reducing inequality, democratising economic and developmental opportunities, and improving public services. Lesson 2: Defined public interest, as opposed to political ambition or the facilitation of vested interests, should be the principal driver for change. Deep and genuine engagement with the public, not just their representatives, must constitute the starting point, not the finish line, and be non-negotiable. Furthermore, a distinction must be made between public need — the genuine reasons which justify change — and public demand — which can be easily manufactured through weaponising algorithms and orchestrated street power. The stronger the mechanisms for filtering out political noise and faux narratives, the greater the likelihood of neutralising proxy gerrymandering on public opinion. Administrative boundaries are not sacrosanct and must be viewed as mechanisms designed to serve evolving and defined public interest. Lesson 3:There needs to be absolute clarity on the purpose of the proposed changes, an agreement on the precise problems the changes set out to resolve, and complete transparency on plans. Vague, stylised assertions around improving governance and service delivery, and absence of transparency on both purpose and process, will only serve as a petridish for political and social discontent and extended, simmering disputes. Three other insights, peculiar to Pakistan’s context are important to highlight: first, the functionalisation and empowerment of local governments must be embedded within the debate on new provinces, as these are not mutually exclusive discussions. Second, it is necessary to look under the hood of how provinces themselves create administrative units, based as they are on administrative fiat rather than legislative approval — otherwise, we risk repeating the mistake made under the 18th Amendment’s Article 140-A, which left it to the provinces to establish independent local governments (they didn’t). Third, rejigging old solutions wrapped inside tired narratives and tactics (administrative fiat, holding illegal/ mala fide referendums, relying heavily on ethno-linguistic nationalism as a criterion) will be unfortunate. To move forward, a three-step roadmap is proposed: 1: Establish a ‘Commission for Citizen-Centric Change’ as a multi-stakeholder, cross-party, independent, and empowered institutional arrangement to lead the process. As part of its work, it should be tasked with extensive public engagement, and the conduct of technical analysis to determine criteria, weigh options, and ensure transparency and knowledge management. 2: Institute a three-dimensional ‘Public Interest Test’ framework that includes an assessment of the public benefits and whether they meet citizen aspirations and socioeconomic needs; a fiscal viability review to determine financial and economic sustainability; and an institutional readiness mapping to measure state capabilities and agility. 3: Test this framework and institutional arrangements by targeting one province. Punjab is the most obvious case for review given its size and the ongoing debate on a south Punjab province. It should be used as a policy lab. Results emerging from this lab should inform a nationwide scaling.Indeed, it is time to get serious. The writer is a former adviser to the chair of the G77 and China.
articles.author: Farrukh Moriani

articles.title: Seeing red in Iran
articles.content: IN the run-up to yesterday’s US mid-term elections, it became obvious that, almost four decades after the Cold War ended, the ‘spectre of communism’ Marx and Engels identified in the 19th century still haunts Western consciousness. Islamophobia might have been the most prominent weapon, but it was accompanied by diatribes against Marxists and communists, invariably directed against people who are neither. For good measure, some of them are simultaneously derided as Islamist jihadists. The American establishment’s obsession with the communist threat, real or imagined, dates back to the early 20th century, and has served as a guiding principle of its foreign (and domestic) policy since the Truman era. One of the CIA’s first interventions, against Iranian democracy in the early 1950s, was justified as a blow against communist influence, even though the popular nationalist Mohammad Mossadegh was barely left of centre. Furthermore, the communist party Tudeh had initially misidentified him as a mole for US interests, recognising only belatedly that his oil nationalisation was in Iran’s interest. The party was decimated in the wake of the CIA-guided coup that re-established the Shah’s reign, under the aegis of Savak, MI6, and Mossad. The survivors fled abroad, mostly ending up in East Germany, although many underground operatives remained in situ, and retained some influence in the military arm of the state. Thus, when Tudeh resurfaced in the lead-up to the 1979 revolution, it wasn’t starting from scratch. It participated in the mass surge against the tyrannical Shah, but, unlike the militant Mujahideen-i-Khalq and others on the left, acknowledged the Khomeini phenomenon as a legitimate expression of the popular will. That helps to explain why Tudeh briefly became the main opposition in a milieu dominated by the Islamic Republican Party. It’s unlikely this arrangement would anyhow have lasted long, but things came to a head in 1982-83. The US today faces its own Great Game fallout. The saga is laid out in entertaining detail in espionage specialist author Ben Macintyre’s recently published Redwood — a fascinating, albeit somewhat breathless, account of the defection in Tehran of a senior KGB officer, Vladimir Kuzichkin, the Soviet point man for contacts with Tudeh and a network of spies. In Macintyre’s reading, Kuzichkin was disillusioned with his corrupt colleagues, as well as with the Soviet polity, but above all, it was his impotence that drove him to risk approaching MI6, expecting Western medicine to offer a cure. (Viagra was more than a decade away, but MI6 was able to organise a discreet circumcision.) More significantly, Kuzichkin passed on to MI6’s Ian McCredie his list of Iranian contacts and details of communications with Moscow. MI6 shared them with the CIA, which was unable to operate in Iran at the time, and the latter insisted on sharing them with Iran’s intelligence agencies. Iran had only recently released the hostages taken at the US embassy, but while the American cold warriors might not have been fans of the clergy, in their blinkered worldview the communist threat was paramount. MI6 was happy, as always, to play second fiddle. The suspicion was that Moscow’s arms and gold were preparing Tudeh for a coup that could pave the way for a Soviet invasion, as in Afghanistan, and further tilt the Cold War imbalance towards communism. By 1982, it should have been obvious to Moscow that the Afghan occupation was going awry — thanks largely to the CIA’s covert war via Pakistan. Macintyre does not mention Zbigniew Brzezinski’s role, through the CIA and regional assets, in luring the Red Army into its biggest folly. But, given the state of affairs in the neighb-ourhood, it’s unlikely Moscow would seriously have contemplated a sim ilar misadventure in Iran. Nonetheless, it was decided to impart Redwood’s information to the Iranian authorities, and the chosen venue was Islamabad, courtesy of the then ISI chief Gen Abdul Rehman Akhtar. Even though senior elements of the Iranian leadership — including Ayatollah Khomeini, parliamentary speaker Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, and prime minister Mir-Hossein Mousavi — had their doubts about the imminence of a communist coup attempt and advised restraint, the president Ali Khamenei and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps chief Mohsen Rezaei favoured haste, leading to thousands of arrests and mass executions, alongside torture and televised ‘confessions’. As in Afghanistan earlier this century, the US is today confronted, in part, with the consequences of its own Great Game machinations. But ask any surviving cold warrior, and most likely they’ll still contend it was a price worth paying for keeping the world safe from communism. Many of us, meanwhile, awaiting this week’s election results, look forward to the impending demise of the American empire.
articles.author: Mahir Ali

articles.title: The Antalya test
articles.content: THIS year’s climate summit, to be held in Antalya next month, comes at a critical juncture. COP31 will be shadowed by UN reports that the Paris Accord target of keeping world temperatures below 1.5 degrees Celsius will be missed. Geopolitical tensions have compelled countries to divert attention and resources from combating climate change. With greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions on the rise, 2026 will go down as the hottest year on record. An extraordinary El Niño could worsen matters. For the first time in the history of the climate convention, two states, Türkiye and Australia, will share roles and responsibilities. Türkiye will have the presidency of COP and Australia has the new role of ‘president of negotiations’. Both co-hosts have been active in preparing the ground for making Antalya a success. Australia hosted a pre- COP summit in Fiji recently, with participation of leaders from the Pacific Island nations — a region most vulnerable to climate change and now also threatened by a menacing El Niño. Türkiye has linked COP31 priorities to cities, waste and a just energy transition — three critical areas for realising Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) in developing countries and accelerating climate action. Cities account for roughly 70 per cent of global energy-related Co2 emissions. Waste, particularly food waste and landfill methane, is the third-largest source of human-caused GHG emissions globally. Yet waste management has been treated as a footnote in climate talks. Antalya has the potential to correct that, embedding circular economy principles and urban climate planning into formal UNFCCC processes. The Just Transition agenda is equally central and considered a political requisite for phasing out fossil fuels to protect households and livelihoods. The world requires a framework for adequate and timely climate funds. Branded as the ‘COP of implementation’, the Turkish presidency wants it to be a meeting where actions take precedence over promises, raising hopes of a breakthrough on climate finance — the main stumbling block. The previous two COP meetings took important decisions on climate finance that beg implementation. COP30 agreed to a triple adaptation fund, and decided to raise $1.3 trillion by 2035 for overall climate action. If achieved, it will be the largest fund-raiser in history for a single purpose. Unfortunately, the prospects of achieving these targets by the stipulated timeline appear bleak. The financing gap for adaptation keeps rising and is now touching $365 billion a year as per United Nations Environment Programme reports based on extrapolated needs expressed by developing countries in their NDCs and National Adaptation Plans. More worrying is the decline in international public adaptation finance flows to $26bn in 2023 from $28bn the previous year. This, according to UNEP, creates a massive funding deficit where actual adaptation needs are 12 to 14 times greater than available financial flows. Pakistan requires huge amounts of funds for implementing its climate policies. Its NDC 3.0 submitted last year puts its total climate investment needs for 2025-2035 at $565.7bn and adaptation needs at $235.2bn, a daunting challenge for one of the world’s most climate-vulnerable countries, with a minimal per capita footprint of 3.2 tons. The predicament of other climate-vulnerable countries is no different. Mobilising such large funds will be impossible for the cash-strapped economies of the Global South given the complicated and lengthy processes of global financial instruments. The world needs a robust framework that unlocks adequate, timely, and accessible funds for effective climate action in vulnerable countries. Expectations from Antalya include est- ablishing the implementation structure for three significant outcomes of COP30’s Belem package. First, the two-year work programme to follow up the implementation of financial pledges of $1.3tr and mobilisation of $300bn by developed countries for adaptation; second, the Global Climate Finance Accountability Framework to bring coherence to fragmented pledges and ensure transparency in financial disbursement; and third, the Just Transition Mechanism to support workers and communities dependent on brown industry. The Loss and Damage Fund, though operationalised, faces its first real test of replenishment at Antalya. Currently, the fund has mobilised less than $1bn — a small fraction of what is needed in this area. While COP31 will not negotiate any new global deal, it offers an opportunity for Pakistan and other developing countries to explore options for collaboration with development partners. International support will only be effective when complemented by credible national adaptation frameworks, and a pipeline of bankable projects. The writer is a career diplomat, a climate expert and a former director at UNEP.
articles.author: Jamil Ahmad

articles.title: Electoral reform
articles.content: THEparliamentary committee on electoral reform, which is being constituted by the National Assembly Speaker, sounds promising. But the public has watched this exercise many times before. None has delivered a credible election. Therefore, the legislators must ask why the laws already on the books keep failing before they start redrafting new statutes. Pakistan’s current electoral framework appears to be sound. The Election Commission of Pakistan enjoys constitutional protection, financial autonomy, and a bipartisan process for appointing its leadership. Yet both the 2018 and 2024 general elections ended in bitter disputes over the credibility and transparency of results. Neither the government nor the opposition has made a serious effort to initiate consultations on a replacement for the current chief election commissioner whose tenure ended nearly two years ago. The real problem is the gulf between the statute book and what happens on polling day, not the laws. Legitimacy depends on consistent enforcement, genuine institutional independence, and a shared willingness to respect the rules. Nevertheless, the committee can still close several gaps in the current legislation. First, provinces routinely delay local government elections for years, citing the need to amend local laws. This stops the ECP from discharging its constitutional duty when the term of an elected LG expires. Parliament should bar provincial governments from altering local election laws once a council completes its tenure, so that the ECP can hold polls within the constitutional time frame. Second, campaign finance rules are full of loopholes. Under the Elections Act, 2017, candidates can dodge spending limits by claiming that third-party expenditure was not authorised by their campaigns. Spending limits mean little if a candidate can disown whoever spends on their behalf. If money is spent to advance a candidate’s campaign, the candidate should answer for it. Third, financial scrutiny must be extended to foreign funding to both parties and individual candidates routed through affiliated non-profits and offshore accounts for the sake of transparency. Last but not least, the caretaker government model needs an overhaul. Letting political parties haggle over nominees does not guarantee neutrality, which must be tested against the record of those appointed. The law should have clearer safeguards against conflicts of interest and political bias among caretaker officeholders, so that transitions are not open to partisan interference. These fixes are worth making. But they will count for little if meddling in polls and selective enforcement continue to be unchecked. Domestic and international observersraised serious concernsabout the 2024 results process. Until parliament deals with the interference that feeds public distrust, further amendments will change very little. The country does not need a new rulebook. It needs institutions and actors who follow the one it already has.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Competing demands
articles.content: THE climate crisis is becoming harder to confront as the world develops new ways to consume scarce resources. At an SDPI event, Senator Sherry Rehman drew attention to the intersection of climate change, AI, energy security, and geopolitical tensions. Her concern was that governments can no longer afford to address these challenges in isolation, as decisions in one area increasingly affect another. AI, for example, is often presented as a means of improving efficiency and accelerating economic growth. Yet the data centres powering it require enormous amounts of electricity, while their cooling systems can place additional pressure on water supplies. The rapid expansion of this technology is raising questions about where the necessary energy will come from and how its environmental costs will be managed. Beyond the demands of new technology, geopolitical conflicts and uncertainty over energy supplies are also encouraging governments to prioritise immediate economic interests over emissions reduction. The latest UNEP projections suggest that existing national climate commitments, even if fully implemented, would still leave the planet heading towards approximately 2.6°C of warming by 2100. Together, these pressures are making it harder to reconcile economic priorities with the urgent need to limit global warming. For Pakistan, these competing demands present a challenge. The country wants to attract investment in AI and digital infrastructure while struggling with expensive electricity, water shortages, and growing exposure to extreme weather. These ambitions need not be abandoned, but their resource requirements cannot be overlooked. New data centres must be assessed not simply for the investment and employment they promise but also for their impact on the power grid and local water supplies. Renewable energy could help meet demand, provided expansion is backed by reliable infrastructure. Yet the responsibility for managing these pressures cannot be equally divided. Wealthier economies have greater capacity to manage the environmental impact of digital expansion. Countries such as Pakistan, meanwhile, face climate risks with fewer resources. Integrated thinking should, therefore, shape domestic planning and global climate talks. Pakistan must press for a fairer distribution of climate responsibilities while ensuring that its own technological goals do not further strain the resources its people depend upon.
articles.author: Editorial
